blocks.text: 03-OFF / offers Goes here. Direct-response offer structuring and mechanics. Covers lead generation offers (soft, hard, negative, deferred), premium and "bait piece" strategy (information products, perceived value vs. fulfillment cost), pricing psychology (installments, price anchoring, the "drop-in-the-bucket" technique, loss leaders, good/better/best tiering), risk reversal and guarantees (length, conditionality, coverage, activation, the "unfair advantage"), urgency/scarcity ratchets, and the structural design of order devices/reply elements (reducing friction, multi-option checkboxes). Topics. offer mechanics / soft vs. hard offers, negative and deferred response options, modified bill-me options, B2B vs. B2C payment nuances. premiums and bait pieces / information products (white papers, CDs, reports), perceived value vs. actual cost, naming conventions for lead magnets. pricing strategies / the "drop-in-the-bucket" technique, price anchoring against expensive alternatives, installment payments, the "magic of a dollar/penny", loss-leader cross-selling, good/better/best tiering. guarantees and risk reversal / unconditional vs. conditional framing, guarantee length and activation, "unfair advantage" guarantees (keeping digital goods post-refund). urgency and scarcity / specific date vs. generic time limits, early-bird pricing, strict quantity limits. reply elements / order form structuring, yes/no/maybe response stickers, reducing form fields.

Lead-Gen Offer Types: Soft offers (free info/brochures), Hard offers (consultation/appointments—avoiding the word "salesperson"), Negative offers (giving a reason why they aren't interested), Deferred offers (asking to be contacted at a specific future date).

The "Drop-in-the-Bucket" Technique: Pricing formulas that contrast the product price against a much higher frame of reference before revealing the cost (e.g., comparing a $39 product to a $500/hour consulting rate).
Payment Fractioning: Breaking lump sums into smaller mental hurdles (e.g., turning a $297 annual fee into "just 81 cents a day" or offering four quarterly payments of $39).
Bait Piece Value Assignment: Assigning a distinct dollar value (e.g., $29) on the cover of a free premium and validating it by selling it at that price elsewhere.

The "Unfair Advantage" Guarantee: Allowing customers to receive a full refund while explicitly telling them to keep the delivered product (highly effective for zero-marginal-cost digital goods) to dramatically lift initial conversion rates.
Modified "Bill-Me" Offers: Structures for B2B continuity where an invoice is sent, but the product (or premium) is withheld until payment clears.

Skip. General advertising theory, brand awareness messaging, or generic copywriting advice (e.g., grammar or minor word choices) that does not fundamentally alter the mechanics or terms of the offer itself.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (standard unconditional guarantees, basic pricing clarity), 85% growth (complex bait pieces, deferred negative offers, installment psychology, drop-in-the-bucket framing). Volume. ~500 words.

OceanofPDF.com Introduction What Albert Einstein Can Teach You About Improving Your Advertising Results _____________________________ “The irresistible offer is an identity-building offer central to a product, service, or company where the believable return on investment (ROI) is communicated so clearly and efficiently that it’s immediately apparent you’d have to be a fool to pass it up.” — Mark Joyner _____________________________ I assume you are a small-business owner, marketing manager, Internet marketer, direct marketer, ad agency creative director, copywriter, product manager, advertising manager, or any other marketer concerned with generating leads and orders, and not just communicating brand messages. In this book, we will explore ways to dramatically improve response rates to your promotions anywhere from 10 percent to as much as 900 percent — just by creating and testing different offers. As you know, an “offer” is simply what your prospects get when they respond to your ad or mailing — combined with what they have to do to get it. In its simplest form, an offer might be “Call us toll-free for a free booklet on adjustable beds.” The booklet is what prospects get. Making the phone call is what they have to do to get it. “Give your reader something to do and make it easy for him to do it,” writes G. Lynn Sumner in his book How I Learned the Secrets of Success in Advertising (North Audley Media). “Tell him where to get what you have to sell, how much it costs — and why he should do it now.” An irresistible offer promises prospects something so compelling or desirable that they can’t help but call, write, or go online to get it. “The irresistible offer is an identity-building offer central to a product, service, or company where the believable return on investment (ROI) is communicated so clearly and efficiently that it’s immediately apparent you’d have to be a fool to pass it up,” writes Internet marketing pioneer Mark Joyner. Or, to paraphrase Marlon Brando in The Godfather, it’s an offer your prospect can’t refuse. What’s the biggest difference between general advertising and direct marketing? In my view, it’s that direct marketers recognize the critical importance of the offer, while general marketers, by and large, do not. More than that, direct marketers focus their efforts on driving the largest volume of qualified prospects to accept their offers. General advertisers spend their time agonizing over the messaging in their ads and finding creative ways to express it. General advertisers are concerned with image and brand. What image of the company does their advertising convey? Are consumers aware of their brand and what it stands for? What brand messages do they want to communicate? How can they make those brand messages memorable? Direct marketers focus on presenting compelling reasons why consumers should buy their products right then and there, as well as overcoming any objections the consumers may have. They are concerned with the action they want the consumer to take — and how to get him or her to take it. General advertisers sit in conference rooms, brainstorm what they want to say about the product, and then spend large amounts of money communicating those messages in their advertising. They often ask consumers for their opinions of products, brands, and advertising through focus groups, surveys, and other market research. Direct marketers do not assume they know what consumers want to hear or what will sell best. They test everything: lists, media, key sales appeals, headlines, envelope teasers, direct-mail package size, mailing formats, Web page colors, banner designs, and offers. Many direct marketers eschew market research in favor of live tests of actual promotions, believing the only opinion expressed by consumers that has any meaning is the one they vote on with their checkbooks and credit cards. So which approach is better — the brand-driven approach of the general advertiser or the offer-driven approach of the direct marketer? A recent study by The Kern Organization found that when marketing sells the offer instead of the brand, it generates approximately 10 times more orders and sales: (Source: Target Marketing, 4/08) Figures are based on direct mail promotions to sell offers with high lifetime customer values including cable TV subscriptions, long-distance and cell phone service. The wisdom of stressing the offer in advertisements has been known for well over a century. In 1902, three years before he wrote his groundbreaking paper on the theory of relativity, a young Albert Einstein ran newspaper ads offering his services as a tutor in math and physics. The ads prominently offered a “free trial lesson” — showing that free offers really are a smart marketing tactic! The two areas in your promotional copy where you can get the most leverage — the greatest lift in responses and orders — are the opening and the closing. The opening is mainly the headline and lead of your copy, as well as its graphic design and presentation. In his book The Architecture of Persuasion, Michael Masterson shows you how to write compelling headlines and leads. The closing of your copy is largely the offer and its presentation. In How to Create Irresistible Offers, I’ll show you how to craft strong offers that make your marketing make more money for you. I do have one favor to ask. If you’ve used a great offer that works, why not send the promotion to me so I can share it with readers of the next edition of this book? I also welcome your comments and questions on How to Create Irresistible Offers. You can reach me at: Bob Bly Copywriter / Consultant 590 Delcina Drive River Vale, NJ 07675 Phone: (201) 505-9451 Fax: (201) 573-4094 E-mail: rwbly@bly.com Web: www.bly.com OceanofPDF.com 1 Offers That Bring in a Flood of New Leads There are two major categories of direct marketing: lead generation and order generation. Order generation, also called “mail order,” seeks to generate an order for a product directly from the promotion. Mail order is “one-step marketing,” because you make the sale in a single step. As Bill Bonner of Agora Publishing describes it, “You send strangers a letter, and they send you money.” Lead generation seeks to produce an inquiry or sales lead — to get qualified prospects to metaphorically raise their hands and say, “Hey, I might be interested in this product. Tell me more.” Lead generation is “twostep marketing.” The first step is sending the promotion and generating the inquiry. The next step is following up on the inquiry and closing the sale. Strong offers are critical to the success of both lead generation and mail order marketing. The strategic planning, selection, and testing of offers can make or break a campaign, regardless of how well designed or well written the piece is. In this chapter, we’ll look at the offers that work best for lead generation. Creating a Simple Offer That Works A typical offer for a lead-generating promotion might be “Call us tollfree for a free catalog on adjustable beds plus a copy of our free booklet: How to Get a Good Night’s Sleep.” The catalog and booklet are what prospects get. Making the phone call is what they have to do to get it. As a rule, the more valuable and risk-free the offer seems to the reader, the better your response. The presentation of the offer — the copy used to describe it, the graphics, its position in the promotion — is also important. Usually, the more you emphasize and stress the offer in copy and graphics, the higher your response rate. Another rule of thumb: The clearer and more understandable your offer, the better your response. The lack of a clear, distinct offer can significantly depress response. The simplest, most popular offer in lead generation is probably the offer of a brochure describing the product or service. In direct mail, this typically reads: “For a free brochure on the Widget 2000, complete and mail the enclosed reply card today.” What the prospects get is a brochure describing the product. What they have to do to get it is fill in and mail a reply card. The offer of a free brochure can and does work for numerous products and services. However, you can often come up with a much more attractive offer — one that will get many more people to be interested in your proposition and respond to your ad or mailing. In lead generation, there are four fundamentally different types of offers: soft, hard, negative, and deferred. Get More Leads With a Soft Offer In a soft offer, the prospect requests some type of printed material that is mailed or shipped to him or downloaded online as a PDF document. The prospect makes this request by using a reply card or other response mechanism that does not require face-to-face or other personal communication between him and the seller. For example: For a FREE copy of our white paper on Best Software Audit Practices, complete and mail the reply card today. Want our latest catalog? Call toll-free 800-XXXXXXX. We’ll rush a copy first-class as soon as we hear from you. To download our new free white paper, “Calculating ROI From ERP Implementation,” click here now. The important thing to note about the soft offer is that it’s the most painless, risk-free way for the prospect to raise his hand, get in touch with you, and say, “I may be interested — tell me more” … without having to subject himself to sales pressure of any kind. The typical soft offer in a direct-mail letter reads as follows: “If you’re interested in learning more about what Product X can do for you, just complete and mail the enclosed reply card for a free brochure.” The prospect checks off a box on a reply card and mails it to you. You mail the requested literature back. The prospect has expressed interest, responded, and received information without making personal contact. The soft offer appeals to prospects who do not have an immediate need and are “just looking,” and to those who have an immediate need but want to gather preliminary information without speaking to agents or sales reps. The soft offer generates a high level of response, because there is no sales pressure or risk of being pitched by high-pressure sales types. It promises details that can be reviewed by the prospects at their leisure. Many marketers mistakenly believe that all people who respond to soft offers are just collecting brochures or white papers, and are therefore not real prospects. For this reason, they avoid soft offers. They say, “If the prospect doesn’t pick up the phone and call me, she’s not really interested. I don’t want to waste time and money sending her expensive color brochures that she’s just going to file or throw away.” While there’s some validity to this point of view, it usually turns out not to be true. Soft leads can be extremely profitable, and often the conversion rate is just as good as it is with hard leads. In a survey of IT professionals, for instance, 57 percent said that white papers influenced their buying decisions. For most promotions, the best strategy is actually to give the reader a choice of several offers, not just a soft offer or a hard offer. Target Your Best Prospects With Hard Offers The opposite of the soft offer is the hard offer. A hard offer in lead generation requires or results in face-to-face or other personal contact between buyer and seller. Whether in person or on the phone, the seller has the prospect “captive” for purposes of doing some selling. In the hard offer, the prospect typically calls or writes the advertiser to arrange a meeting, demonstration, initial consultation, or appointment. There is direct person-to-person contact between buyer and seller — initially over the telephone and, usually, later face to face. During these contacts, outbound telemarketing representatives or salespeople attempt to persuade prospects to buy the product or service being offered. Examples of hard offers: * To get a no-obligation estimate for adding a new family room or den to your house, just complete and return the Free Estimate Request Form enclosed. * For a free analysis of what you’ll need to save to put your children through college, call XXX-XXX-XXXX today. The hard offer is ideal for prospects who have a serious interest, an immediate need, or a desire to buy something fairly soon and want to sit down and talk with vendors. The prospect responding to a hard offer, especially if doing it by telephone, typically feels a fairly urgent need to gather more information for an immediate or upcoming purchase. With a hard offer, the prospect is taking a definite (if tentative or uncommitted) step toward purchasing the product. A soft offer, by comparison, gets more of a “Let me look you over” or “We’ll wait and see” response. Turn a “No” Into a “Maybe” With a Negative Offer In addition to soft and hard offers, there are two other basic categories of offers: negative and deferred. The negative offer reads as follows on the reply element: Not interested right now because: (Please give reason — thank you.) Typically, reference to the negative offer is made in the P.S. or elsewhere in the body of the sales letter, using the following language: P.S. Even if you are not interested in [name of product or service], please complete and return the enclosed reply card. Thank you. The negative offer provides a response option for people who qualify as prospects — that is, they have a need or problem your product addresses — but, for whatever reason, are not ready to take the next step in the buying process: getting more information on your product. A negative offer instructs the reader to respond even if she does not want to learn more about your product, which is disarming and unusual. By using a negative offer option, you can often get a response from a small portion of your prospects. That response can be increased by giving the reader a logical reason to reply: P.S. Even if you are not interested in [name of product or service], please complete and return the enclosed reply card so we can give your free [whatever is being offered] to another person on our list. Thank you. The negative offer should be used when you are testing a mailing on a new product, service, or offer you haven’t promoted before using direct mail. The reason you use the negative offer is that, without it, if you get a low or no response to your mailing, you don’t know whether it’s the mailing piece that’s ineffective or the product, service, or offer that isn’t right for the market. With the negative option, people will tell you why they are not interested in your offer. Perhaps the price is too high. Or your technology is not compatible with the systems they are already using. Or they don’t like your type of product or don’t use it. This information not only helps you readjust your marketing plans, it demonstrates that the mailing was unsuccessful for reasons other than ineffective copy and design — something that’s good to know if you’re the person who wrote or designed it. A second benefit of the negative option is that it can slightly increase your overall response rate. You might object and say, “But all the people who check the negative option box have told us they are not prospects.” But quite the opposite is often true: If people take the time to tell you why your offer isn’t right for them, they may be prime prospects. They’re telling you they have some sort of need, but your product as described in the mailing doesn’t seem quite right … and that they want you to get back to them with a product, service, or offer that is right for them. Actually, your product or service may be ideal for them, but your ad or mail copy may not have communicated that effectively — or they misunderstood or didn’t read carefully enough. That’s okay. By completing the negative offer option box, your prospects have set themselves up for follow-up and closing by a skilled salesperson. If you have ever been a salesperson, you know the most difficult prospect to sell is the one you can’t reach — the one who never responds to your letters, never returns your phone calls, or says he is not interested but won’t say why. A prospect who fills in the blank space on your reply card where it says “Please give a reason why you are not interested” has framed a specific objection, which can be overcome with the proper selling argument. Get Non-Responders to Reply With a Deferred Offer A deferred offer is a variation on the negative offer. Here’s how it’s phrased on the reply element: Not interested right now. Try us again in (month/year) The deferred offer encourages responses from prospects who do not have an immediate need but may have a future requirement for your product or service. Some of these prospects won’t check off the soft offer option box (“[ ] Please send me a brochure”) because they think, “If I check off this box, they’re going to follow up with a phone call and pester me. I don’t have a need right now.” The deferred offer option box says to this prospect, “If you have no immediate requirement but may have a future need, you can use this box to let us know that you have a future need, without getting calls and annoying follow-up from salespeople now.” When do you use the negative as opposed to the deferred offer option? Use the negative offer when you are testing a new offer or when you think many prospects might not respond for specific reasons. Use the deferred offer when you think a significant number of prospects might need your services at some future date rather than right away. Increase the Odds of Sales Success With Multiple Offer Options A common mistake in lead-generating promotions is to have only one offer option. In most instances, you should have two or three options. In lead generation, the best results usually come from having three offers: a soft offer, a hard offer, and either a negative or a deferred offer. At minimum, you should have both a soft and a hard offer, with one of the two being primary and the other secondary. The primary offer is the one you hope your prospects will respond to and the one you emphasize in your copy and graphics. For example, if you want a face-to-face meeting with your prospects, you would urge them to call and arrange an appointment. A “free, no-obligation initial appointment” would be your primary offer, the one you stress in your letter or e-mail. The secondary offer is included to give those prospects who will not take you up on your primary offer a second reason to respond. If a prospect is not willing or ready to take you up on your offer of a free initial meeting, introduce the secondary soft offer at the end of your ad or letter copy. (“P.S. For a free special report outlining six tax-saving strategies offered by our firm, just complete and mail the enclosed reply card.”) _____________________________ Your Primary Offer: Hard or Soft? Which offer should be your primary offer? Make your soft offer — the offer of free literature or information — the primary offer when: You know requesting a brochure or catalog is the typical first step in the buying process in your particular industry or field — and that circumventing that step would be counterproductive. You feel many prospects would be reluctant to meet or talk with you, so you need some sort of brochure or other literature to create a reason for them to respond to your mailing. Your product or service is complex and requires a lot of explanation that is best communicated in a standardized written format, such as a brochure or data sheet. You have limited staff for telephone contact with prospects, and your operation lends itself more to the mailing of a standardized inquiryfulfillment brochure or package. Your prospects are far away, and you do not have regional branch offices or sales reps who can call on them in person. You have a great brochure or inquiry-fulfillment kit already in place that has proven its ability to (1) screen out unqualified prospects and (2) sell effectively to qualified prospects. Industrial equipment manufacturers are a good example of marketers who stress soft offers. Their prospects — engineers and purchasing agents — require a lot of detailed information on technical products before making a buying decision. This technical information is communicated more easily in a printed brochure than over the telephone. Also, having a brochure on an industrial product is standard practice in the industry. Most purchasers won’t buy without having a brochure or other technical literature in their files. So a logical next step in industrial direct mail and ads is the offer of such a brochure or catalog, at no charge. The hard offer should be the primary offer when: You would prefer to get a phone inquiry rather than a written inquiry because your salespeople are more likely to close when they receive a hot lead via an inbound telephone call. You believe sending printed material, such as a brochure or catalog, is an unnecessary step that only gets in the way and slows down the selling process. There is not a lot of information or detail to communicate about your service or product, and you can sum it up quickly and easily in a twominute phone conversation. You have a free trial offer or other special offer that enables prospects to try your service or product on a small scale for free or for a nominal fee, and you feel you can get prospects to accept this offer if you can sell them on the phone or face to face. Your product or service is unique, unusual, and difficult to communicate in printed material, and you can more easily communicate it in person, either over the phone or via demonstration. Your audience is not comprised of readers or information seekers. An example of an industry that doesn’t tend to use brochures is adult vocational training. One such marketer told me, “We have learned through experience that offering a brochure is a waste. To sell the prospect on taking our program, we have to get him to come to our facility in person for a free introductory class. Otherwise, it won’t work.” _____________________________ Once you have the soft and hard offer options in place, you add either a negative option (if you want to learn why prospects are not responding as you had hoped) or a deferred option (if yours is the type of product or service that is likely to be bought at a future date rather than immediately). How will the response be split? In one mailing I did to promote my freelance copywriting services, the following letter generated a 10 percent response: Dear Marketing Professional: “It’s hard to find a copywriter who can handle directresponse, business-to-business, and high-tech accounts,” a prospect told me over the phone today, “especially for landing pages, white papers, direct mail, and other long-copy assignments.” Do you have that same problem? If so, please complete and mail the enclosed reply card and I’ll send you a free information kit describing a service that can help. As a freelance copywriter specializing in direct marketing, I’ve written hundreds of successful ads, sales letters, directmail packages, landing pages, e-mail marketing campaigns, brochures, case studies, feature articles, press releases, newsletters, and websites for clients all over the country. But my information kit will give you the full story. You’ll receive a comprehensive “WELCOME” letter that tells all about my copywriting service — who I work for, what I can do for you, how we can work together. You’ll also get my client list (I’ve written for more than 100 companies) … client testimonials … biographical background … samples of work I’ve done in your field … a fee schedule listing what I charge for sales letters, white papers, and other assignments … helpful article reprints on copywriting and marketing … even an order form you can use to put me to work for you. Whether you have an immediate project, a future need, or are just curious, I urge you to send for this information kit. It’s free … there’s no obligation … and you’ll like having a proven copywriting resource on file — someone you can call on whenever you need him. From experience, I’ve learned that the best time to evaluate a copywriter and take a look at his work is before you need him, not when a project deadline comes crashing around the corner. You want to feel comfortable about a writer and his capabilities in advance … so when a project does come up, you know who to call. Why not mail back the reply card TODAY, while it is still handy? I’ll rush your free information kit as soon as I hear from you. Regards, Bob Bly P.S. Need an immediate quote on a copywriting project? Call me at (201) 385-1220. There is no charge for a cost estimate. And no obligation to buy. Of the total response, most people (more than 90 percent) checked the soft offer box (“Please send more information”) on the card. Fewer than one in 10 (less than 10 percent) checked the hard offer box (“Give me a call”). Only a couple selected the deferred offer. I can convert between 10 and 25 percent of leads from this letter to sales within six months of receipt of the inquiry … if I want that much business. Interestingly, there is no difference in the quality of the lead (seriousness of the prospect) between those who check the soft offer box and those who check the hard offer box: Percentage conversion to sales is the same in both categories. Almost all of the response to this mailing is from the reply card. I give my telephone number in the letter, but do not encourage phone calls. (I prefer to speak to prospects only after they have received a complete package of information about my services.) I do not give a fax number or encourage fax responses. People check the deferred offer box (“Not interested right now”) infrequently, and I mail so few of these letters that I can’t give you a statistical result. Qualitatively, however, I can tell you that having the third box for the deferred offer has paid off. I can recall specific instances where a prospect checked the “Try us again” option, and, when I followed up, I found they did indeed have a specific project in mind to be started at a specific date. Immediate follow-up with literature and a later phone call at the time requested resulted in a sale in at least two cases. OceanofPDF.com 2 Hook More Prospects With a “Bait Piece” — and Double Your Response _____________________________ “The free booklet offer is so effective and so important that, for most marketers seeking to generate leads, I think it’s a mistake not to have such an offer as part of their promotions.” — Bob Bly _____________________________ The most effective method of increasing the response rate of a leadgeneration campaign is to use a “bait piece.” The term bait piece refers to free information the advertiser offers in a mailing piece or e-mail to generate a higher number of inquiries. The word bait is used because the free content is given not just to educate the reader (as the reader is led to believe) but to “hook” the reader by generating a response or inquiry, which can then be followed up by telephone or field sales personnel. To make this strategy work, the content of the bait piece should be relevant, valuable, desirable, and specific to the prospect’s interests and needs. There are a number of ways to enhance the soft offer by giving away a bait piece. The most popular, and probably still the most effective, is with a free booklet, special report, white paper, or other printed content. Where does the free bait piece fit into the sales cycle? The diagram above tells the story. Your initial e-mail, direct mail, or other promotion offers the bait piece. Some of those who read your promotion respond by asking for the bait piece. You fulfill these inquiries by sending the bait piece along with sales materials (e.g., a brochure) on your product or services. Then you follow up. Depending on the nature and cost of your product or service, anywhere from 10 to 35 percent or more of those requesting the free bait piece will ultimately do business with you. _____________________________ Here is a fact many direct marketers do not know: Just by adding a free bait piece to your offer, you can often double the response to your ads and mailings over what the response for essentially the same ad or letter copy would be without the free information offer. _____________________________ Why are free content offers so effective? For several reasons. In fact, this is one of the few direct-response rules that works almost every time. In virtually every campaign where I have added a free booklet offer to the marketing program, sales lead generation has increased substantially and marketing costs were reduced. I know of few other strategies that are so basic, simple, and easy to use while consistently delivering such excellent results. Despite this, many marketers avoid using free booklet offers, based largely on the following erroneous beliefs. If you are not using the bait piece strategy because of one of these fears, this list may be helpful in overcoming your particular objection. The five erroneous beliefs are: 1. “It’s a cliché.” The number one reason marketers avoid free booklet offers is that they think it’s old hat and are looking for something original. They say to me: “Offering a free booklet isn’t original. Can’t you think of something more creative?” My answer is simple: So what if it’s old hat? So what if it’s a formula? The reality is, it works consistently and repeatedly for companies in all industries. The fact that free booklet offers are not original is true but unimportant. What’s important is that they will generate more leads per ad or mailing, producing more inquiries and more sales while lowering marketing costs. 2. “It’s overused.” Another common objection is, “I like the idea, but free booklet offers are so overused in our industry. Take a look at the magazines serving our niche, and you see free booklet offers in every other ad. Every other mailing I receive offers a free booklet. So how could our offer compete with all this clutter?” This argument makes sense but is refuted by experience. While there are some marketing techniques that do lose effectiveness in the face of clutter and overuse, the free booklet offer is not one of them. In fact, the opposite is often true: Prospects in a particular industry become accustomed to seeing ads with free booklet offers and eagerly seek out such ads in their trade publications. If your ad lacks such a bait piece, prospects are more likely to pass it by. 3. “Our competitors already offer a free booklet.” The natural tendency is to think, “Our competitor has already published a booklet on the topic we were thinking of, so they’ve beaten us to it. There’s no sense going ahead with ours.” Free content offers can establish you as a thought leader in your industry and increase response to your marketing campaigns. But the bait piece itself is almost never a branding strategy or unique selling proposition (USP). The fact that your competitors also give away bait pieces is largely irrelevant and certainly not a reason to avoid the technique. If anything, it demonstrates that the tactic works in your market. The right strategy is to go ahead with your own booklet and either (1) choose a topic that’s different but still helps promote your product or (2) choose the same topic and produce a report or booklet that’s better. How do you make your booklet better? Give tips and strategies the competition does not. Include a helpful glossary, charts, conversion tables, bibliography, checklists, names and addresses of resources, graphs, and other useful references. Use pictures and illustrations to make your point clear. Reveal inside information and details the competition keeps secret. Even if the topic is similar, select a title that’s clearly different from the competition’s. Having the same or a similar-sounding title confuses prospects and isn’t good for either you or your competitor. Without a free booklet offer, your prospects are likely to respond only to your competitors’ ads, which do offer booklets, while skipping over yours. Adding a free booklet offer helps ensure that you, too, will hear from prospects with a need to buy what you are selling. 4. “My prospects already have too much to read.” The fourth argument against free information offers is either “My prospects already have too much to read, so the last thing they want is another booklet or report” or “My prospects are not readers.” While it is true that many prospects already have too much to read, they will still seek out and send for yet another booklet or report if they perceive that it contains information that is relevant, helpful, and tailored to their needs. A prospect may have six inches of paperwork stacked in his inbasket, yet if his most pressing problem is cutting energy costs in the plant, he will respond to an ad or direct-mail package offering a free report on “6 Proven Ways to Cut Energy Costs in Your Plant This Year.” Ideally, you want your prospect not only to send for but also to read your booklet or report. However, even if a prospect sends for but does not read your free information, the bait piece offer has still done its job: It’s generated an inquiry from a prospect who would otherwise have tossed your ad or mailing aside. Therefore, the fact that your prospects are too busy or not inclined to read the material you send is not a good reason not to offer such information. The key is to overcome inertia and get them to respond. Once you receive the inquiry, you can start the selling process to convert the lead to a sale. But with no response, you get nowhere. And free booklet offers increase response. 5. “If we give away free content, we’ll generate a large volume of poor-quality leads from freebie seekers.” If this is a concern, you can qualify the leads more up front and generate a better quality lead using some or all of the following techniques: Charge a nominal fee for your catalog, brochure, or other literature. Ask the prospects to answer a lot of questions about themselves. Make them fill out a survey or complete a questionnaire. Make the prospects pay the postage on the return envelope or postcard. Tell prospects you will not fulfill inquiries if they do not provide their phone number. Say, “Serious inquiries only, please.” Do not stress guarantees, money-back offers, free offers, and risk-free trials or estimates. If you offer a premium, do not send the gift in response to the inquiry. Instead, tell prospects they will be given the gift in person when they meet with your salesperson or that the gift is sent when they make a purchase. Bait Pieces: Free or Fee? In most cases, I recommend that you do not charge for your bait piece. If you’re offering a booklet or report to generate leads, the booklet or report should be free. Unless your primary business is selling books or reports by mail and you are offering this booklet or report to build your mailing list, charging for it will dramatically decrease your response rate and slow down the flow of leads. And that defeats the reason for offering the bait piece in the first place. One argument for charging is the theory that people who pay for the booklet or report are better-qualified prospects. This isn’t true (unless, again, your main business is selling books or reports by mail). For businessto-business lead generation, you can qualify prospects by asking them questions (e.g., “What type of business are you in?” or “What is your immediate need?”) on your ad coupon or direct-mail reply card. But does asking them to pay $5 for your booklet make them more qualified to buy your widget? I don’t think so. In fact, it only serves to prevent a lot of qualified prospects who would have requested your widget booklet if it were free from doing so. (The reason is not the cost but the added trouble of writing a check and sending it to you.) The basic offer options for bait pieces are as follows: Booklet or report free to prospects who call or mail the reply card. Booklet or report available free only to qualified prospects. Booklet or report free with self-addressed, stamped envelope. Booklet or report free with self-addressed, stamped envelope and $1 or $2 to cover handling. Booklet or report for $5 (or whatever you want to charge). Booklet or report free to qualified prospects; $5 (or whatever you want to charge) to the general public and others who are not qualified prospects. CD or DVD free, with $5.95 charged to credit card for shipping and handling. If the cost of printing and distributing booklets is a real hardship for you, you can recover that cost by requesting that the reader supply a selfaddressed, stamped envelope and $1 or $2 to cover shipping and handling. But I don’t recommend this. For 99.99 percent of marketers, the free booklet offer should be just that — entirely free. SR, one of my mentors in freelance copywriting, told me an interesting story about charging prospects for information. Many years ago, SR promoted his freelance copywriting services with small display ads in The Wall Street Journal. The ads offered a “copywriting information kit” that included reprints of helpful marketing articles. SR’s small ad generated dozens of inquiries when he offered the information kit free. Many of the inquiries were serious. Some turned into business. A few, of course, were from freebie seekers who had no interest in hiring SR and just wanted the free articles. This frustrated SR, because it wasted his time and money to fulfill those inquiries. To cut down on freeloaders, SR changed the ad, requiring respondents to send him a nominal sum — just three dollars — to get the information kit. The response dwindled from dozens of inquiries to two or three per ad … and no business. Charging for his bait piece certainly did away with freeloaders. But it also discouraged legitimate prospects from inquiring about his services. Lesson learned: With rare exceptions, the bait piece should be free. That’s especially true today, when offering a print, audio, or video bait piece as an online download reduces fulfillment costs to practically zero. The soft offer is designed to generate leads from qualified prospects — folks who could surely benefit from your product but are not ready to buy it. It does this by offering them information: a product brochure, white paper, or other free content. The hard offer captures inquiries from hot prospects who have an immediate need and want to buy now instead of later. It results in a face-toface or telephone meeting between the seller and the potential buyer. A marketing manager once told me that prospects are like submarines: They are submerged most of the time and surface only occasionally. The soft offer ferrets out prospects who are submerged by getting them to raise their hands and say, “I might be interested. Tell me more.” But the hot prospect has surfaced. She is actively looking for a product or service to solve a specific problem, fill a pressing need, or handle a particular application. The hard offer is the weapon that helps us spot hot prospects “swimming on the surface” and reel them in. In this chapter, we’ll review five time-tested rules for creating winning hard offers that capture more hot prospects that you can meet with and convert into sales. Rule 1: Do Not Involve “Salespeople.” A typical hard offer in lead generation is a check-off box on the business reply card or ad coupon that says, “Have a salesperson call me.” By choosing this offer option, the prospect is saying, “I have sufficient interest in your product or service that I am willing to have your salesperson make a presentation to me or at least chat with me over the phone for a few minutes.” This is a more aggressive, active response toward initiating the next step in the selling process than the soft offer of “Send me a brochure.” “Have a salesperson call” is probably the most widely used hard offer in lead generation. It paves the way for the in-person sales visit that, for many marketers, is a crucial step in getting the prospect to buy their product or service. In many cases, however, very few prospects select this offer option. Reason: Prospects don’t view salespeople as helpful or beneficial. In fact, the word salesperson signals to the prospect that sales pressure will be exerted — something most prospects want to avoid. The word “salesperson” has a negative connotation, implying that the prospect will be subjected to high-pressure selling tactics aimed at benefiting the seller, not the buyer. The solution is to repackage the “Have a salesperson call me” offer, using skillful copywriting and a change in tactics, to convert what is perceived as a sell job into what is perceived as a meeting that will be beneficial and helpful for the prospect. In a nutshell, this is done by replacing the words sell and sales with words that are more prospectoriented. To start with, do not use the term salesperson when referring to the person who will contact or follow up with the prospect. Replace salesperson with any of the following (or create your own title, as appropriate): Account Representative Senior Consultant Technical Specialist Account Manager Account Supervisor Industry Specialist Program Manager Program Planner [name of product] Specialist [description of application] Specialist For example, if you are selling financial services, don’t say, “Have a sales representative call.” Instead, say: “Have a financial consultant call” or “Have a financial planner call” (if your salespeople are truly financial planners). If you are selling a relational database, say, “Have a database specialist call.” If you are a consultant teaching firms how to sell by using social networking, say “Have a social networking specialist call.” Rule 2: Do Not Offer to Do a “Sales Presentation.” Do not use the words sales call, sales pitch, or sales presentation when referring to the initial appointment you are seeking with the prospect, because of the negative connotation of the word sales. Instead of a sales call or sales presentation, suggest to prospects that they contact you to arrange one of the following: Initial appointment Free, no-obligation consultation Free estimate Free analysis Needs assessment Audit Exploratory meeting Evaluation of their requirements Initial planning session Free demonstration Free executive briefing Free seminar Your hard offer might now read: Please have a technical consultant call to arrange a free analysis of my network requirements. I understand there is no cost for this initial analysis — and no obligation. If you phrase your offer this way (or in a similar fashion), you will get more response than if you simply say, “Have a salesperson call” or “Call me to arrange a sales presentation.” Why does this technique work so well? If you think about it, you’ll realize that any initial contact between buyer and seller is not merely a selling opportunity for the marketer — it has value to the buyer independent of whether he buys the product or service. For example, if a printer makes a presentation and gives you a price quotation, that price information is of value even if you do not hire the printer, since it provides a benchmark against which you can judge other quotes. You might also gain some helpful pointers on the print production process, and the printer is not compensated for giving this knowledge to you unless you actually hire him to do the job. Say you have an initial meeting with a financial planner during which you ask questions about investment options, your financial situation, and so on. In order to convince you that she is knowledgeable, the financial planner will probably answer many of those questions. You can put that information to work even if you decide not to hire that particular person. Therefore, the initial sales meeting has value inherent in the meeting itself and independent of the product or service. The strategy of offering a “free consultation by our expert,” as opposed to the traditional “sales presentation by our salesperson,” simply recognizes this inherent value — and it increases response by highlighting the value of the initial meeting or contact itself, rather than asking for a sales opportunity. Rule 3: Do Not Charge for the First Meeting. If you are actively prospecting for new customers or clients, I assume that you need the business. If you always had more leads than you could ever hope to handle, you would not need to proactively generate more. Given that you want or need new business, you can get more appointments by offering the initial meeting or conversation for free. Some prospects may represent an account so potentially lucrative that it is worth traveling to meet them. With prospects whose value is more marginal, you may decide that the only way you can “meet” with them for free is over the phone. When your prospect requests an initial meeting, make it clear that the meeting or consultation is free. This alone may give you an advantage over your competitors, some of whom may charge for the first meeting. For instance, we once called three landscape architects to get a quote on landscaping the front lawn of a home we owned. All three have good reputations in our county. Two were willing to visit us, inspect the property, and give us a free quote. The quote included a free preliminary drawing, showing us the landscapes they proposed to create for us. The third vendor explained that he charged $100 for a landscape drawing, so his quote could not include one unless we paid his fee. “I can still come to your home and give you an estimate for the landscaping for free,” he said. “You just won’t get my drawing until you retain me.” His position seemed reasonable, so we had him come and give us a free estimate. But when we reviewed the three quotes, the other two had beautiful drawings and his had none. Given that the pricing was fairly equivalent, he had no chance of winning our business. We chose one of the other landscaping firms. If you are in a field where it is not unusual for some vendors to charge for initial meetings, estimates, or preliminary recommendations, your prospects may assume you charge too. So your marketing copy must make it clear that you do not charge, as this gives you an advantage over your competitors. Especially when your offer sounds too good and generous to be true, prospects become suspicious that there is some hidden charge or implicit agreement requiring them to buy something. Always stress in your copy: “This initial consultation is absolutely free, with no obligation of any kind.” Rule 4: Add Value to the Initial Meeting. Offering the initial meeting for free is good. But it’s even more attractive if you convince the prospect that the initial meeting has a high value. People like getting free stuff, but they don’t get too excited when that stuff is always free and widely available. If you convince them that you are giving away an exclusive and valuable service worth $100 or $1,000 for free, they become much more eager to acquire it. For instance, one of the more interesting hard offers I wrote copy for was a free “network topology analysis” by Timeplex, a manufacturer of multiplexers, switches, and hubs for telecommunications and data networks. When a prospect accepted this offer, we’d send a sales representative to visit. Using proprietary network design software and his laptop, the rep would sketch the prospect’s network layout or “topology.” Then, the rep would click an “optimize” button. The software would reconfigure the network by adding Timeplex multiplexers. By doing so, it reduced the number of voice and data lines. The software, as I recall, calculated the monthly cost savings from this line reduction, as well as the ROI of adding the Timeplex network elements. Just by meeting with the Timeplex “networking specialist,” the prospect could get “a FREE network topology analysis that can reduce your monthly line costs 10% to 20% or more.” That made the offer hard to resist, and extremely successful for Timeplex. Rule 5: State That There Is No Obligation to Buy. Tell the prospect that your offer is free and without obligation. State it in your sales letter and again on the reply form. People can be skeptical of free offers. They have heard and heeded the old saying, “If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.” Let your prospect know that there are no strings attached. The prospect wants assurance that agreeing to meet with you — or even replying to your promotion — does not obligate him in any way to buy from you or pay you any money. Don’t assume that your prospects understand this to be so. It is also referred to as “cash with order,” though almost no customers send cash. Most pay by check or credit card. The seller ships the product only after payment is received via check, money order, credit card, PayPal, or another method of payment. Use of a hard offer eliminates credit and collection problems because there is no billing. Everyone pays up front. By comparison, the soft offer in mail order selling is the classic “billme” offer. Here, the prospect can order and receive the product with no money up front. The seller sends a bill and is paid later. The Offer Should Not Be an Afterthought When creating a direct-response promotion, many copywriters give the closing copy — especially the formulation and working of the offer — short shrift. The writer simply picks up the boilerplate from previous promotions, without thinking through whether the offer and its wording make sense. Often, they don’t. More and more we see offers that are confusing, deceptive, unfair, or illogical — if we look carefully. Here’s an example: A number of publishers permit the new subscriber to cancel at any time and receive a prorated refund on what they call “unmailed issues.” By that they mean the following … Say your annual subscription costs $96. It entitles you to 12 monthly issues, which works out to $8 per issue. After three issues, you cancel. That means nine issues that you paid for have not been mailed to you and, now that you are canceling, will not be mailed to you. So you are entitled to a $72 refund on those unmailed issues. But here’s where it can get a bit confusing. If the publisher offers both a bill-me option (soft offer) as well as a payment with order option (hard offer), such a prorated refund guarantee actually gives his customers an incentive not to take the hard offer and pay up front — the opposite of what the publisher desires. Say the customer checks the “bill-me” option for a monthly newsletter, gets his first issue, and then writes “cancel” on his invoice. The publisher doesn’t send him a bill for one issue, nor does the publisher ask for the magazine or newsletter back. So the customer gets a free issue. But if the customer pays in advance and then cancels after the first issue, he theoretically gets a refund for eleven-twelfths of the subscription price (for the 11 unmailed issues) and therefore ends up paying for the issue received. (I have talked with many publishers about this. Some give the customer a full refund. But a surprising number actually give only a refund for the 11 unmailed issues less the cost of the one issue sent.) Why should the bill-me customer get a free issue but not the paymentwith-order customer? It doesn’t make sense, considering a cash-with-order customer is more desirable than a bill-me customer. How can you fix this problem? Offer a full money-back guarantee within the first 30 days, then a prorated refund thereafter. That way, everyone gets the first issue free if they decide not to become subscribers, whether they enclose payment with their order or chose the bill-me option. Make Your Offer Crystal Clear To paraphrase Ralph Waldo Emerson, it is not enough to state your offers clearly enough to be understood. You must state them so plainly that they cannot possibly be misunderstood. Reason: Nothing is worse for your business reputation than a customer who did not understand your offer and feels he is being cheated when you refuse him a refund. Let’s take the famous “lifetime guarantee.” On the surface, this seems simple and direct. For as long as you own the product, you can return it for a refund at any time. But really, at any time? Of course you can return it if it wears out or falls apart. But what if it becomes damaged through your own negligence? What if it works fine but you are simply bored with it and wish to have a newer model or different color? Does lifetime mean the lifetime of the seller or the lifetime of the buyer? The wording in lifetime guarantees is at times ambiguous, unclear, or even misleading. For instance, in subscription marketing, the old standard lifetime offer used to be “a prorated refund on the unused portion of your subscription” or on “unmailed issues.” No problem there. You knew that if you cancelled after six months and the newsletter cost $100, you would get $50 back. Now, promotional copy says the publisher offers “a full refund on the unused portion of your subscription.” Are they offering 100 percent of your money back? No. By “full,” they mean the full amount of the cost of the unmailed issues. Again, for a $100 subscription cancelled after six months, that’s a $50 refund. But when consumers read “full,” they may interpret that to mean “all my money back.” If you really are giving back the subscriber all of her money, make it clear — e.g., “We’ll refund your entire subscription fee in full” or “We’ll refund every penny you paid.” Another gray area is the offer of a free issue. Many subscription offers with a 30-day money-back guarantee promote the first issue, sent within 30 days, as a “free issue.” In reality, that issue is free only if you do not become a subscriber. If you do subscribe, you are paying for that issue, because it is one of a total of 12 you will get as part of your one-year subscription. So for those who pay and do not request a refund, there is no free issue. In that case, “free issue” is not wholly accurate. More correctly, the offer should say “risk-free issue” or “no-risk issue.” To make it a truly free issue, the publisher would have to give them the first issue plus, if they subscribe, 12 more issues — a total of 13 issues for the price of 12. The solution is to phrase the bill-me option check-off box this way: “Bill me. But that’s going to a lot of trouble to get a free special report. Asking for the money before you send the premium requires more of a commitment from the subscriber. The result: fewer replies from people who have no intention of subscribing but just want something for free. The more choices you ask the buyer to make, the more she has to think about before making her buying decision. And a decision deferred is a decision not made. In consumer mail order, you can get away with having a hard offer only, and indeed many consumer mail order marketers do not offer a billme option. They want to avoid the hassle and headache of collections, and so require payment for the product up front. Also, with the price tag on many consumer mail order purchases being so low, it often doesn’t pay to go after deadbeats who keep your product but don’t pay your bill. The deadbeat realizes it’s not worth your time and effort taking him to court for a $12 past-due balance, and therefore doesn’t feel an urgent need to respond to your dunning letters. I know from decades of experience that pay-ups are a huge issue for marketers selling products with bill-me offers. The true measure of profitability is not how many orders you get, but how many of those buyers pay for what they ordered. Some buyers quickly return the merchandise. Less scrupulous buyers keep it without paying. So while bill-me offers usually lift front-end response, the gross revenues, once you subtract for the no-pays, can actually be less than cash-with-order. So you do not necessarily need to have a bill-me option for consumer mail order marketing. In many cases a bill-me offer will increase gross response, but the question is, how many of those who order on a bill-me basis ultimately pay up? A test gives you the surest answer. Many consumer mail order firms, especially smaller ones, do quite nicely without a bill-me option. They know it’s easy for the consumer to write a check, send a money order, or charge it to her American Express, Visa, or MasterCard. I run a small but profitable part-time mail order business selling books, manuals, and audio albums to writers and would-be writers, and we have not had a problem with our payment-with-order policy. In business-to-business direct marketing, on the other hand, I believe it is a mistake, in most instances, not to include some type of soft bill-me offer to supplement the hard pay-up-front offer. Why? Because the recipient is ordering for his or her company, not for personal use. Most B2B companies are not set up to issue advance checks. Their usual procedure when making a purchase is to issue a purchase order, receive the product, be satisfied with it, get an invoice, then pay you when they are ready — hopefully in 30 days but more often in 60 or 90 days. If your selling method forces business buyers to go against their company system, they may decide that buying from you is too difficult or just not worth the aggravation and effort, and take their business to a competitor who is more flexible about payment terms and options. If you demand payment up front, the prospect may not even know how to get the accounting department to issue and send you an advance check. Therefore, when selling to businesses, you should offer both a soft bill-me option as well as a hard payment-with-order option. Fortunately, there is a way to structure an offer that meets your business customer’s needs as well as your own requirements. It is done by extending a traditional hard offer (payment up front), as well as a second one that is conditional, rather than a pure “soft” bill-me offer. The traditional soft offer says, “We’ll send you our product and bill you. If you like it, you can keep it and pay the bill. If you don’t, you may return it, tear up the invoice, and you will not owe us any money.” Perhaps your product is expensive or easily damaged, and you are afraid that people will take advantage of you by ordering the product, keeping it, and not paying for it. One solution is to use a modified bill-me offer, in which you agree to send an invoice but do not ship the product until the invoice is processed and payment is received. This would read as follows: [ ] Bill me. (NOTE: Product not shipped until payment is received.) The modified bill-me is similar to a soft offer in that it allows the prospect to respond without enclosing any payment and to receive an invoice from you that he can put through the system for payment. At the same time, it is similar to a hard offer in that the product is not shipped until it is paid for. A variation of the modified bill-me is to agree to ship the product right away but to withhold shipment of any gift item or other premium until payment is received. There is a danger, if your premium is too attractive, that people will send for your product on a bill-me basis just to get the premium, then return the product and keep the free gift. To prevent this, you use a modified bill-me offer as follows: [ ] Bill me. (NOTE: Bonus Gift is shipped when payment in full for your order is received by us.) Even if you allow prospects to keep the premium if they return the product, this modified bill-me offer cuts down on freebie seekers. It requires ordering and paying for the product in order to get the gift, and few will go to that trouble just to get a free item from you — unless the premium is truly fantastic. You can go even further and state in your offer that, if they don’t want to keep the product and decide to return it for a refund, they must return the premium as well as the product. This provides an added degree of protection and is useful when the premium is fairly costly to you. Another way to modify the bill-me offer so that you reduce the number of prospects who send for the product and don’t buy it is to ask prospects to initial or sign the order card or provide a purchase order number or actual purchase order. For example: [ ] Bill me. Our purchase order number is: ______________ Signature (required for all bill-me orders): ______________ For phone and online orders, you can’t get a signature, but you can still ask for a purchase order number. I recommend that you avoid requiring prospects to send you an actual purchase order. The purchase order number itself is sufficient. If you insist on getting an actual purchase order, you will lose sales from prospects who are too busy to generate the paperwork. In general, your mailings should never force prospects to read a lot of instructions or fine print or fill out a lot of complicated paperwork. The more work you force your prospect to do to respond to your mailing, the lower your response will be. Consumer magazines are more likely than newsletters to offer merchandise premiums. For many years, Business Week gave away a free solar calculator with a subscription to the magazine. Sports Illustrated offered a free video of the photo shoot for its annual swimsuit issue. 6 Steps to Irresistible Offers The more of the following characteristics your offer incorporates, the more irresistible it will be, and the higher your response rates: 1. Different or unique. The best offers are fresh and new. When copywriter Bill Jayme wrote the direct-mail package that launched New York magazine, he proposed a sweepstakes. Sweepstakes had long been used to sell magazine subscriptions, but none had ever offered the prize Jayme dreamed up: dinner at Gracie Mansion with New York City’s mayor. Most investment newsletters offer free special reports as premiums. The Sovereign Society, a newsletter on offshore investing, offered something different: a free Swiss bank account — a gift not given by any other investment newsletter. Most business magazines offer either discounted subscription rates or standard premiums like special reports, tote bags, or calculators. Advertising Age had a successful control where the premium was a ceramic coffee mug. Coffee mugs are nothing special. But this one was imprinted with a mock-up of an Ad Age cover. If the subscriber was Jan Smith, the headline on the mock issue of Ad Age was personalized to read: “Jan Smith Chosen as Marketing Genius of the Year.” 2. Desirable. An unusual offer works only if it’s something people really want. The Sports Illustrated swimsuit video is a great example. Every red-blooded American male who wasn’t dead would have liked to see it. Sex sells! Another example: A publisher was selling a loose-leaf service on how to manage Novell NetWare local area networks. Response rates doubled when a new direct-mail promotion offered a disk with free software — a collection of utilities for Novell networks. The 100 percent increase in orders confirmed that these software programs were tools network administrators obviously wanted to get their hands on. The outer envelope teaser read: “Yours FREE! — 5 Powerful Programs to Help You Manage Your Novell NetWare Network More Efficiently and Easily — See Inside for Details on This Special TimeLimited Offer.” On the other hand, when a financial newsletter mailed a renewal promotion that offered as a premium a pack of playing cards with the editor’s picture on them, it flopped. No surprise. Who would want that? 3. Has a high perceived value, especially in relation to your fulfillment cost. Free software has traditionally worked well as a premium. Software has a high perceived value in relation to the cost of the goods. In a store or online, software packages can easily sell for $49 to $300 or more. Yet a CD with code on it can be duplicated for about a dollar. That’s why the promotion offering a pack of playing cards with the newsletter editor’s picture on them didn’t work. After all, how much do you pay for a deck of playing cards at your local stationery store? About a dollar, right? Therefore, the perceived value of the playing cards was only a dollar — hardly a motivator to renew a newsletter subscription that costs $79 a year. In a promotion tied in with their sponsorship of the Olympics, IBM offered a special IBM Olympic pin as a premium. In reality, the pin probably only cost (and was worth) a buck or so. But the mailer copy hinted that it could become a collectible, creating the impression of potentially high value. 4. Dramatizes the brand or USP. The symbol for offshore investing has long been Swiss bank accounts. Therefore, the offer of a free Swiss bank account with a subscription to The Sovereign Society supported and dramatized the newsletter’s USP: making money and increasing privacy by investing offshore in things like Swiss bank accounts. Even when the offer does not at first glance seem closely related to the product, a clever copywriter can find a connection. Example: Years ago, Newsweek offered a free radio as a premium for new subscribers. It would seem that a radio was a poor choice for a premium: In the news area, radio and magazines compete with one another. But copywriter Milt Pierce used the differences between these media to make a logical connection between the premium and the product: Dear Reader: What’s the fastest way to get the news? It’s on the radio. That’s why Newsweek wants you to have — as an introductory gift for new subscribers — this superb AM/FM radio. But what’s the best way to get the news? You won’t get just headlines and a rough outline of the news, with Newsweek; you’ll get the news in depth … 5. Easy to take advantage of. You should make it as easy and convenient as possible for the prospect to accept your offer. How? To begin with, offer multiple response mechanisms: toll-free phone number … fax number … a hyperlink to a landing page (see www.thelandingpageguru.com) … e-mail … even (gasp!) a postal address. Different prospects respond in different ways. In a direct-mail package, enclose a fax-back form or business reply card (BRC) with your sales letter. If you want customers to enclose payment with their order, or privacy is a concern, also include a business reply envelope (BRE). In a print ad, consider including a coupon or a bind-in BRC opposite the advertisement. On the Web, your landing page should ask for the minimum information from the prospect when collecting leads. If you are building your opt-in e-list, ask for name and e-mail address only. When you have multiple fields for the user to complete, use an asterisk (*) to indicate which are mandatory, and make as many fields as possible optional. Conversion rates decline incrementally for each additional field you force the prospect to fill out. The ease and convenience of accepting the offer can even be highlighted in the copy as a benefit. In a letter selling the Board Report, a newsletter for graphic designers, copywriter Sig Rosenblum makes a benefit out of the fact that the reply element is a BRC: Please complete the card enclosed and drop it in the mail today. It’s already addressed. And the postage is paid. 6. Minimizes the buyer’s risk and obligation. Do whatever you can to minimize sales pressure on the prospect. If you follow up leads by phone instead of with a field sales force, say in your copy “No salesperson will visit.” If you do not follow up leads by phone, say “No salesperson will call.” When offering anything free — a white paper, a webinar, even a brochure — say that it is free. Do not substitute the weaker “complimentary” when writing to a high-level business audience because you think “free” is not professional or will offend them. It won’t. Everybody wants free stuff, and businesspeople and professionals are no exception. A health care agency sent a direct-mail piece inviting doctors to attend a symposium. They did an A/B split test of two versions. The only difference was that B offered a free pocket diary as a gift for attendance. Version B out-pulled version A — with no free gift — six-fold. Busy doctors were persuaded to give up an afternoon by a free pocket diary that cost about a dollar! Does the buyer have to agree to sit through a presentation or demonstration or complete a survey? If he is not required to take further action once he accepts the offer, note this in your copy by saying: “There’s no obligation … nothing to buy … and no commitment of any kind.” How Many Premiums Should You Offer? Should you offer a single premium, two premiums, many premiums? In his book Secrets of Successful Direct Mail (NTC, 1992), the late Dick Benson said: “Two premiums are frequently better than one.” Newsletter and magazine subscribers and other information product buyers especially like multiple premiums. To promote one of my books, we offered almost a dozen free special reports — all downloadable PDFs, so they cost us nothing to deliver. The promotion worked, and the book became the #1 nonfiction bestseller on www.amazon.com, with more than 900 orders in a single day. In an online promotion for Men’s Health, Rodale offered 10 free reports: Assign a dollar value to special reports you give away as premiums by putting a price in the upper right corner of the front cover. Demonstrate that the price is real, not made up, by putting up a page on your main website where you sell all your bonus reports in an online shopping cart for the actual price on the cover. You will get some orders from your site visitors, so you can say in your copy: “We are not making this price up. We actually sell this report at this price on our website.” Michael Bell of Phillips Publishing suggests that the total value of the multiple reports you are giving away should exceed the price of the newsletter subscription. That way, the buyer is getting his money’s worth with the premiums alone, so, in a sense, he is getting the newsletter free. Premiums can be used to get customers to make their first purchase as well as to motivate them to continue buying. Franklin Mint had a brilliant offer for their Civil War chess set. The customer signed up to get one piece per month. After purchasing all 32 pieces, the customer got a free chessboard. This gave the buyer incentive to collect the whole series. Gevalia offers a subscription service for monthly delivery of gourmet coffee. One incentive they’ve used to get people to sign up was a 12-cup coffeemaker free with their first order. Here are a few additional observations and rules of thumb from Benson’s book concerning offers: Sweepstakes will improve results by 50 percent or more. A credit or bill-me offer will improve results by 50 percent or more. Memberships renew better than plain subscriptions by 10 percent or more. The addition of installment payments for items over $15 will increase results by 15 percent. If you have to choose only one, premiums work better than cash discounts. Subscriptions sold at half-price for at least eight months will convert at renewal time just as strongly as subscriptions sold for a full year at full price. Offers of subscriptions giving a choice of terms (e.g., one year vs. two years) will pull more gross dollars but 10 percent fewer subscriptions. Offering an incentive to pay cash when you offer both cash and credit options reduces net response. The Drop-in-the-Bucket Technique for Overcoming Price Resistance Have you ever been shopping for a major purchase, and when the salesperson told you the price, you said incredulously, “What? HOW much!?” This phenomenon is known as “sticker shock.” In sticker shock, the prospect is so put off by the purchase price that he is nearly traumatized. This is a bad sign for the seller, because a prospect in sticker shock can seldom be convinced to buy. The reason the prospect suffers from sticker shock is not because of the high price. It is because the seller has failed to communicate the true value of the offer. To overcome this, you can use what copywriter Mike Pavlish calls the “drop-in-the-bucket” technique. With this technique, your marketing copy convinces the prospect that the price you are asking — whatever it may be — is a “drop in the bucket” compared to the value he receives. And, you do this before you give the price. I use it for every offer, not just high-priced products. Reason: Before I give the price, I want to feel confident the prospect won’t be shocked by it. For instance, I sell a $79 e-book of business forms for freelance copywriters. I worried that prospects might think $79 is a lot to pay for an e-book on freelance writing, many of which sell for between $9 and $29 online. To combat this, I built the perception of high value using the drop-inthe-bucket technique. Specifically, I explained that this is not a conventional book, but a collection of forms. I then showed the value of ready-made forms and the money savings they offer. Here is the “drop-inthe-bucket” copy from my landing page for this product: What will my Copywriter’s Toolkit cost you? If I added up all the hours spent planning, writing, testing, and refining the tools in this collection, and then multiplied that by my current hourly rate, it would come to well over $25,000. Of course, you could hire a lawyer to draft some of these forms for you, at about $200 an hour. But most lawyers don’t know or understand the copywriting business. But my Copywriter’s Toolkit won’t cost you $25,000 … or $1,000 … or even $200. Instead, the price is just $79 — less than I charge for just 5 minutes of my time! The Copywriter’s Toolkit is a 140-page e-book … which means it’s available for immediate download. No shipping costs. And no waiting. As a licensed purchaser, you get the e-book as well as unlimited rights to use the forms, model letters, and other tools in the toolkit as is … or customize them to fit your own copywriting business. It’s your choice. Information marketers have long understood the importance of making the price of their products seem like a drop in the bucket compared to what they’re worth. A standard line in marketing copy for information products has been: “Just one idea from this program can pay back its cost 10 times over or more!” If your service helps buyers pass regulatory audits, talk about the cost of failing such an audit — fines, penalties, even a shutdown. If your manual on energy efficiency in buildings cuts heating and cooling costs 10 to 20 percent a year, the prospect with a $10,000 fuel bill for his commercial facility will save $1,000 to $2,000 this year and every year — more than justifying the $99 you are asking for the book. Make an apples-to-oranges comparison. Don’t compare your newsletter to another newsletter. Compare it to another information resource, such as private consultation or expensive training.
