If it were guaranteed for a year, the buyer could use it for a year, return it for a refund, buy the new edition, and repeat the cycle ad infinitum. For directories, I like a 30- day money-back guarantee. Then there is the double-your-money-back guarantee, where a dissatisfied customer who returns a $100 product is entitled to a $200 check from you — $100 to cover the refund and $100 to (presumably) compensate him for his trouble. I know from experience that double-your- money-back guarantees can be very powerful and significantly increase sales. One marketer who sold a workshop to help doctors pass their oral board exams had trouble filling seats — until he added a guarantee promising double their money back if they failed the exam after taking the workshop. Attendance and revenues tripled. Conditionality refers to any conditions or limitations you impose on your guarantee. For example, I am sure you’ve seen promotions where the merchant says they will give you a full refund if the product is returned “in saleable condition.” This makes the buyer wary. How do you define “saleable condition”? The buyer fears that if he returns your book for a refund, you will claim that there is a tiny tear in the dust jacket or a smudge on page 78 and refuse to give him his money. Conditional guarantees sound like a good idea, at least to the seller, but when you use them, you are asking for headaches. Trading services, home business start-up kits, and other educational products often say they will refund your money in full “as long as you show you have made a sincere effort to follow our program.” How could a dissatisfied customer seeking a refund prove that he complied with that condition? Some sellers of business opportunity products and trading systems require the customer to return worksheets, completed forms, or other documents proving they attempted to make the program work for them but were not successful. Buyers fear that, instead of getting a prompt refund, the seller will tell them they did not use the materials correctly and instruct them to go back and try again. Bottom line: Consumers distrust conditional guarantees, and using them can depress sales. The best guarantee is the unconditional guarantee. If your guarantee is unconditional, say so in your marketing copy — e.g., “This is our unconditional, iron-clad, money-back guarantee of satisfaction.” Or “We’ll refund your money in full — no questions asked.” An unconditional guarantee of satisfaction, boldly stated, works equally well whether you’re selling information products or merchandise. “We sold custom-lettered work uniforms by mail,” says Lewis Elwin. “We gave a guarantee of complete satisfaction. There was some concern at first because when a lettered garment came back, there’s wasn’t a whole bunch of options for us. But not many came back on the satisfaction issue. Our experience with small business owners was that most of them were honest.” Coverage refers to the part of the purchase that is covered by the money-back guarantee. For merchandise, the seller typically gives the customer his money back when he returns the product. But does that refund include the shipping and handling fee he paid on top of the cost of the merchandise? If it does not, be clear about that in your copy. Instead of saying “full refund” use the phrase “product refund.” A product refund does not include a refund of the shipping and handling charges. Should you refund shipping and handling? I don’t. Some direct marketers not only refund the shipping and handling charges, they also pay for return shipping of the product from the dissatisfied customer. If it’s a small item, they might include a postage-paid return shipping label with the product. If it’s larger, they may give you a return label for UPS or even send a freight company to take the product back. You will occasionally have a customer who says he tried your product and, not only does he want a refund, he wants you to compensate him for lost time or money spent using it. I am not a lawyer and cannot give you legal advice. So if you run into a problem like this with a persistent customer, you should consult an attorney. But, in general, I would say you are not responsible for any damages beyond the cost of the product except in extraordinary circumstances. (If, for example, the customer uses your shampoo and his hair turns permanently purple.) Guarantee coverage can be an issue for seminar marketers. Will you allow a person to take the entire seminar and, if he is then not satisfied, give him a refund? He may be able to return his workbook and other materials, but he can’t return the seminar itself, because he has already absorbed the information. Some seminar promoters tell attendees that if they are not satisfied, they should let the seminar leader know by the first break on the first day of the event. At that point, they can turn in their materials, leave, and get a full refund. After that, it’s too late. Activation refers to the time period when the guarantee goes into effect, as well as to what the customer has to do to take advantage of it. Does the 30 days for a month-long money-back guarantee start the day the order is placed or the day the product is delivered? Your customer expects it to be 30 days from receipt of goods, and that’s the way your guarantee should be written. Your guarantee should also spell out exactly how to get a refund. Companies selling nutritional supplements by mail, for instance, usually tell the customer that they must return the “unused portion” of the product or “even the empty bottles.” Years ago, a mail order company was selling corncob pipes by mail. Their guarantee was, “If you are not 100 percent satisfied, break the stem off the pipe and mail it back to us for a refund.” This eliminated the trouble and expense of returning the whole pipe, but also emphasized the company’s confidence in its product: If you didn’t agree it was great, they wanted you to destroy it. In his classic ad for “The Lazy Man’s Way to Riches,” the late Joe Karbo made this guarantee famous: “Send us a check and we will send you the product. We won’t cash your check for 30 days. If you return the product within 30 days, we will send your uncashed check back.” This ploy can, in fact, generate incremental improvement in response, giving you another few orders per thousand pieces mailed. However, it may also increase the number of bad checks you receive. At least one major seminar promoter has used a similar guarantee. When you arrive at the seminar venue, there is a table with a pile of checks on it, including yours. If you are not satisfied, you may leave. On the way out, pick up your uncashed check for a full refund of the seminar fee. What happens when a customer wants a refund after the guarantee period has expired? Be reasonable but firm. If someone wants to return one of my products and they missed the cut-off by a few days or even a week, I let it slide. However, if they are asking for a refund months after the guarantee expired, I tell them sorry but it’s too late. If they are reasonable or have been a regular customer, I may offer them a credit for a future purchase rather than a refund. Two More Tips for Strengthening Your Guarantees There are two other things to consider when creating your guarantee: Clarity. Make certain the terms and conditions of the guarantee are clearly stated and spelled out. Be careful about wording that the consumer can misinterpret. For instance, a performance-based guarantee — “If you do not earn extra money trading options with our program, return it for a refund” — sounds good but raises a potential concern. Namely, does it mean that if I DO make some extra money with the product, I can’t return it — even if I only made 10 bucks? Rewrite the guarantee so there is no condition or ambiguity stated or implied: “If you do not make extra money trading options with our program, or you are not 100 percent satisfied for any other reason — or for no reason — just return the program within 90 days for a full refund.” Make it stand out. The guarantee should be graphically emphasized within the promotion. Don’t bury it in body copy or put it in an asterisked footnote in 8-point type. Print the guarantee in 12-point type with a large, bold headline. Put a box or even a certificate-style border around it to make it stand out. Boost Orders Up to 21 Percent With an “Unfair Advantage” Offer E-books and other downloadable PDF information products present a unique problem as far as guarantees and refunds are concerned. With a hardcover or paperback book, if you want a refund you have to return the product. When you do, the seller has the book (which he can resell), you don’t, and you get your money back. But how do you return an e-book? The seller has the original PDF file, so they won’t want or need your copy. Even if you send it, how do they know you didn’t keep a copy on your hard drive? Some e-book sellers require customers requesting refunds to delete the PDF from their hard drive (and, I would suppose, throw away or rip up any printouts of the document). How do they know the buyer has complied? They don’t. Since there is no way to know whether a customer has deleted and destroyed their copy of my e-book, I don’t make them do it. In fact … I tell them they can keep it! Here — taken from the landing page for The Copywriter’s Toolkit — is my standard guarantee for the e-books and other downloadable PDF information products I sell online: _____________________________ Our 100% iron-clad guarantee of satisfaction I totally guarantee your satisfaction with this toolkit. If you aren’t convinced that The Copywriter’s Toolkit is the smartest investment you’ve made in your freelance copywriting business this year, just let me know within 90 days. I’ll send you a prompt refund of your $39. And you can still keep the e-book with my compliments. That way, you risk nothing. So what are you waiting for? To order The Copywriter’s Toolkit on a 90-day risk-free trial basis, just click here now: _____________________________ With such a policy, you might think that people would take advantage of me that and my refunds on e-books would be huge. Why should they pay for my e-books when they can essentially get them for free? The answer is that people are basically honest. Yes, a few do take advantage. But that small number is far outweighed by the increase in orders this strong guarantee generates. The proof: My e-book refund rate is a tiny fraction of 1 percent. And conversion rates increased once I added this copy to my sales pages. Internet marketer David Powers tested it, and found that telling buyers they could keep his e-book either way increased conversion rates and sales by 21 percent. My e-book offer allows the prospect to take unfair advantage of me: If they order the e-book and request a refund, they get it for free. Not only does my offer allow the prospect to take unfair advantage of me, my copy actively encourages them to do so: I’ll send you a prompt refund of your $39. And you can still keep the e-book with my compliments. We call this the “unfair advantage offer” — an offer where, if the prospect accepts it, he benefits unfairly … and the seller incurs loss. The reason to test an unfair advantage offer is its potential to boost response far in excess of the losses incurred from the few customers who exercise the guarantee. Another example: In 1999, one of my clients, a software publisher, was selling a tool that automatically recoded software to be Y2K compliant. When I suggested a 30-day money-back guarantee, the marketing manager balked. In our marketing copy, we explicitly pointed out that they could use the tool during the 30-day trial to recode their systems. The simplest mechanism is to put a time limit on your offer. _____________________________ Michael Masterson, copywriter, entrepreneur, and consultant for newsletter publishing giant, Agora, Inc., has a formula for creating compelling headlines. His Secret of the Four U’s © requires a headline to be unique, ultra-specific, useful (offering a benefit), and urgent. Without a sense of urgency, your promotion may not generate as many responses as you had hoped. And one of the most effective ways to get the prospect to “act now” is to build an element of urgency into your offer. Why It’s Important to Get Prospects to Act Now Instead of Later Your prospect is bombarded by direct mail, e-mails, telemarketing calls, radio commercials, TV spots, and other sales messages and offers. Which means that your best chance of getting her to respond to your offer is to give her sufficient motivation to do it right now, while the piece is still in her hands. There is an old saying among direct marketers: “A decision deferred is a decision not made.” If there is no “respond now” incentive, the prospect may think, “I’ll put this aside and get to it later.” Unfortunately, a directmail package is similar to the Sunday newspaper: If you don’t read it within 48 hours of getting it, chances are you never will. Too many other things surface to compete for your attention. How do you get the prospect to act now instead of later? The simplest mechanism is to put a time limit on your offer. This can either be (1) a specific date (“Offer expires March 15, 2009”) or (2) a generic time limit (“You must reply within 15 days to take advantage of this special free offer”). Both types of deadlines are effective. Which is better? A specific date is good if you have enough control over the timing of your promotion to ensure that delays in printing and mailing don’t make the date obsolete. For instance, you don’t want prospects to get a “Reply by April 15th” mailing on April 21st. If you do not have precise control over timing, or if you print your sales letters in large quantities and mail them regularly, a generic “Respond within the next 15 days” offer may be better. That way, no matter when the mailing arrives, it always works. How long should the time limit be? Which is best? 12 days, 20 days, 25 days, 30 days, two months, or something else? Obviously, the shorter the timeframe, the more pressure there is on the prospect to respond quickly. On the other hand, too short a timeframe may make the prospect feel rushed and uncomfortable. For direct mail, a 15- to 21-day deadline seems reasonable: short enough to motivate action, long enough to allow some breathing space. In e-mail marketing, deadline timeframes can be shorter. E-mails can say “Good this week only” or “Offer expires in 48 hours.” Sending one or two follow-up e-mails reminding prospects that the offer is about to expire as you approach the deadline can be very profitable in generating additional orders. On a landing page, you can have a clock or counter displaying, in real time, the days or hours remaining until the offer expires. Decades ago, Dennis R., a seller of mainframe utility software, used the standard 30-day free trial offer. Then he did a split-test of a 30-day free trial vs. a 60-day free trial. The 60-day offer outperformed the standard 30- day offer by 10 percent. “I concluded that the standard 30-day trial period was not sufficient for a busy IT professional to test our software,” said Dennis. “It would sit on the prospect’s desk for weeks. Then he would put off testing it for another week or two. And by that time, he felt he had to send the software back before he got billed for it. By extending the trial period from 30 days to 60 days, we gave the prospect sufficient time to install and test the software without fear of the free trial period expiring before he did so.” Apparently, 60 days was more than sufficient time for the software trial. When Dennis tested 90 days vs. 60 days, there was no further lift in response. Run all promotional copy past your attorney for vetting, especially time-limited offers. Once you state in your marketing that a certain offer expires on a certain date, you are generally not allowed to extend the offer beyond that date. Word Your Offer for Maximum Impact As I pointed out elsewhere in this book, the language you use to describe your offer can also affect response rates. In another mailing, Dennis tested the 60-day free trial vs. 60-day free use. This time, “free use” outperformed ”free trial” by 15 percent. Dennis concluded that the word “trial” had negative connotations for the IT tech who would be using the software. It meant screwing up batch files and coming in nights and weekends to do the testing. “But,” he said, “everyone wants to use a product — so who wouldn’t like ‘free use’?” For consumer mailings, the offer should require the recipient to reply within the next seven, 11, or 15 days. A common offer in direct mail is an additional “quick-response bonus” — usually a free report or other premium given as an incentive to reply within seven days. Offer expiration moves much faster in television infomercials. Merchandise is often offered on a payment plan — e.g., four easy payments of $19.95. The quick-response incentive is the elimination of one of the payments — the equivalent of a 25 percent discount — for viewers who call within a certain timeframe, usually 20 to 30 minutes. This time element can also be used online to establish a sense of urgency. To promote its annual copywriter’s conference, FastTrack to Copywriting Success Bootcamp & Job Fair, American Writers & Artists Inc. (AWAI) has used a digital display counting down to the expiration date for their early bird registration discount on their bootcamp home page. A variation of the specific timeframe offer is the limited number offer: “This offer is limited to the first 200 people who respond to this letter.” This tactic gets prospects’ attention because they have no idea how many pieces you mailed — and, therefore, are motivated to reply right away to ensure they are one of the first 200. Other variations? The limited offer is most effective when you can give a legitimate, credible reason why the offer is limited. Scarcity can be one such reason: The supply of what you are offering is limited, and, once it is gone, no more will be available. The late Bill Jayme had a clever scarcity line he used in direct-mail packages selling subscriptions to new magazines. It read: “Only so many copies of the premiere issue will be printed — no more.” That statement would be true no matter how many copies were printed. Nonetheless, it communicates a definite sense of limited supply. One computer company offered free prototyping of the prospect’s application. Because prototyping takes time and the company had a limited staff, it could handle only so many prototypes at one time. The sales letter made a point of this, saying, “We urge you to hurry. Based on response to previous mailings, we will get many requests for this free prototyping offer. If you are not one of the first to respond, you may well have to wait longer than we’d both like.” This worked because it was specific, credible, and true. If you don’t have a real reason why the offer is limited, you can invent one, and that can work. But when doing so, respect the intelligence of your prospects. For instance, one mailing I received many years ago told me I had to request a certain report right away because “We have printed only 1,000 copies and supplies are limited.” I suspected, of course, that if requests exceeded 1,000, the company would simply print more. So its act- now incentive lacked credibility for me. (The “limited quantity” offer is especially suspect when the premium can be downloaded as a PDF or MP3 file.) Another effective way to add a sense of urgency is to limit the total number of members, participants, or buyers. For a conference, seminar, or workshop, there really are only so many seats available — and no more. Tell prospects these limited seats are available on a first-come, first-served basis. In a promotion for a new $1,500 financial advisory service, a publisher told prospects that they had to act quickly because he could only take on 1,000 subscribers. Reason: With more than that, he could not make sure his subscribers got good execution on their trades. In his marketing copy he said, quite honestly: “If you apply after I have 1,000 members, I’ll have to return your thousand dollar check to you uncashed, as much as it pains me to do so.” Early-bird discounts are effective for events, and for pre-publication offers for directories, books, and other information products. For a weekend seminar costing $2,497, you might offer a $500 early bird discount, bringing the price to $1,997. For a book or directory selling for $100, even a $5 or $10 pre-publication discount is usually all you need to lift response rates. Give a Gift for Prompt Response A premium is a free gift the prospect gets for responding to your mailing. Does the premium have to relate to the product or service being sold? That depends on whether the purpose of the mailing is to generate leads or to make sales. Dick Benson, a successful consultant and entrepreneur, writes in his book Secrets of Successful Direct Mail (NTC) that it is not necessary for the premium to relate to the product being sold. The most important criteria for premium selection, according to Benson, are the perceived value and desirability of the premium. If the premium relates to the product, fine, but that’s of secondary importance. In lead generation, I agree that having a desirable premium is important, but I put more weight on trying to select a premium related to the product. Also, you have to be careful with premiums because many companies, especially defense contractors and subcontractors, have policies forbidding employees to accept gifts from vendors. In fact, a firm selling custom-imprinted business gifts by mail tested a straight 25 percent discount vs. a 25 percent discount combined with the offer of a free clock radio. Not only did the premium not increase response, it actually depressed it. Why? We can’t know for sure. Perhaps the buyers didn’t want to be perceived as accepting a gift or bribe for giving that vendor his company’s business. Whenever a mail order company attempts to bribe buyers with an expensive gift, some prospects might assume the merchant is inflating the price of their product to make up for the cost of the free gift — and they would rather pay less for the product and not get the gift. In business-to-business marketing, the corporate employee increasingly looks good to management by being a sharp buyer. That means getting the product at the lowest price possible. A larger discount might therefore work better than a free gift intended for personal use. If you do offer a premium to a business buyer, especially one working in a corporate setting, consider making it something related to the product and of value to the buyer’s company. For instance, a publisher selling highpriced technical journals and information databases on CD-ROM offered a free CD-ROM stacker and reader with the purchase of a group of its highpriced CD-ROM—based information products. The premium had high perceived value, was closely related to the product, and made the prospect look like a smart buyer. For lead generation, I think the best use of a premium is to offer something directly related to the product or service. My experience is that unrelated premiums of high value bring in large numbers of “freebie seekers” and other unqualified leads. Modest premiums that are directly related to the product or service increase the total number of responses. While you will always get some inquiries from those people who seem to send for anything and everything that’s free, you will also get a greater volume of qualified leads from good prospects. I personally like the offer of a free booklet or report related to the product or service. This is most often used in the soft offer (“Send for free report”), but it could conceivably be tied to a hard offer. For instance, you can offer an impressive report with the condition that it will be handdelivered by a salesperson. Ricoh did this many years ago when selling fax machines, copiers, and other office equipment via direct mail. You would get a little gift as an incentive for replying to the mailing. Ricoh would call to set up a time for a sales rep to come to your office and demonstrate the machine. The gift item was delivered personally by the sales rep, and you got it only after the demonstration. Samplings, Trial Offers, and Product Evaluations Are All Great Offers Three additional incentives you can use in your marketing are samples, trial offers, and product evaluations: Samples. You offer to render your service or allow the customer to use your product on a sample basis. This may be for purposes of demonstrating your service or product or for analyzing the customer’s needs to determine which of your services or products is right for them. For example, a company selling equipment that turns chemical powders into pellets says in its sales letter, “Send us a five-pound bag of your compound and tell us what size pellets you want. We will run it through our pelletizer and return it to show you the quality of the pellets it can produce.” Graver Chemical makes a similar offer for Ecosorb, a carbon-based filtration medium for purifying water supplies. Their letter states: “Is Ecosorb right for your application? We’d be delighted to evaluate a water sample to see if Ecosorb can handle your particular requirements.” Another company, a computer firm, sells a software program that businesses can use to quickly create customized applications that work with their databases. One potential buyer was skeptical and asked, “How long would it take to develop a so-and-so application for our database using your product?” Instead of answering, the software firm’s rep sat at the computer, started pressing keys, and had the application prototyped and working with the database within 30 minutes. The prospect’s response? “Decision made! We’re buying it!” Trial offers. A trial offer allows the prospect to use your product or service for a specified period at no cost and with no obligation to buy. The pelletizer manufacturer’s letter went on to say that if the sample pellets were satisfactory, they would ship a pelletizer to the prospect’s plant and let them us it for a month with no obligation. Then the company would have the option of sending it back (at the manufacturer’s expense) or buying it. A trial offer can also work with a service. If you have an online database, a long-distance telephone service, or another service where users are billed by the hour, you could offer “30 minutes of use free.” In his book Profitable Direct Marketing, Jim Kobs shows two ads from MCI. The first offers $5 off the prospect’s long-distance phone bill. The second offers 30 free minutes of long-distance calls. The “30 free minutes” offer pulled roughly twice the response of “$5 off” because customers perceived 30 free minutes of long-distance calling to be the greater value. The 30 minutes of free service is, in essence, a free trial of the long-distance phone service. Product evaluations. Similar to the free trial is the product evaluation. The gist of this offer is: “Let us send you the product at no cost, and you can perform whatever technical evaluation is required to help you decide whether it is the right product for you. If it is not, send it back and owe us nothing. If it is, you can buy it for the list price of $X.” One problem with free trials and evaluations is that prospects send for the product — and then, because of inertia, laziness, or lack of time, they don’t do anything with it. One way to overcome this problem is to combine the free trial or evaluation with an incentive to make a buying decision within a specified period of time. For instance: “If you accept our free trial offer and then decide to invest in the so-and-so system within the next 30 days, you will get 10 percent off the regular purchase price.” Mention of this time-limited offer in your ad or mailing can increase overall response. Periodic reminders to prospects via mail or phone during the evaluation period can help get more of them to try the product and increase the conversion rate of leads to sales. Creating Urgency With a Loss Leader Strategy Have you ever read an ad offering a product at a price so low that it seems impossible for the seller to be making a profit? Any item sold at or below cost to attract new customers is called a loss leader. Retail and mail order merchants sell items at or below cost to entice you to their store or get you to place an order. (Retailers refer to these discounted items as “door busters,” because they can whip consumers into such a frenzy that they will literally bust down the door to the store to get one.) Once you purchase the loss leader or door buster, you have made the transition from shopper to paying customer. And the merchant makes his profit by selling existing customers like you additional products with a regular mark-up. An example is mail order coin dealers who offer, say, an American Silver Eagle for $19.95, which they say is “our cost.” They might get 10,000 first-time customers to order the Silver Eagle. With the coin, they send out literature advertising a set of silver coins for $200. Of the initial 10,000 first-time customers, 1,000 buy the set of silver coins, generating $200,000 in revenues. Well, the same loss leader strategy that merchants have been using off line for decades to build their customer lists can now be profitably applied online. Here’s how it works. First, create your loss leader. If you are an online information marketer, it could be an e-book. This e-book should have wide appeal for all segments of your market. The topic should be one that all your customers will find interesting enough to make them want to own the e-book. And be sure it is a truly valuable product. No matter what your intent is, you always want to give your customers great value for their money. That way, they’ll come back to you for more information again and again. Assign a $39 list price to the e-book, for reasons I will make clear in minute. Next, approach your affiliates — other online marketers that you have a commission agreement with — and suggest that they sell your $39 e-book to people on their lists for $19, giving them a special $20 discount offer. Tell your affiliates that you won’t pay the customary 50 percent commission. Instead you’ll give them 100 percent commission for every book that’s sold. That’s right. They get all the money. Reason: If you give them the usual 50 percent commission on the $19 sale, their cut would be only $9.50 — too little to interest them. But 100 percent commission on a $19 sale is equivalent to a 50 percent commission on a $38 sale. And the fact that you are giving them all the commission makes them stand up and take notice. This is why I suggested assigning a retail price of $39 to the e-book. It allows you to offer the consumer a $20 discount, which has strong appeal, and still give the affiliate a $19 commission per sale, which also has strong appeal. What you end up with is a win, win, win situation. The customer gets a great $39 product for $19. The affiliate gets 100 percent of the sales. And you get a valuable list of subscribers. Where to Feature the Offer in Your Copy The offer must be featured prominently on the response device. (In Chapter 9, I will give you copy and graphics guidelines for creating winning reply elements that highlight the strong offers you build.) Of course, the offer is usually mentioned elsewhere in the copy, too. For an offer that is strong but standard, we typically write copy describing it in the closing section of the promotion. The more compelling or unusual the offer is, the more prominently you should feature it. A mailing for the McGraw-Hill Chemical Engineer’s Book Club featured an unusually generous offer: a free copy of Perry’s Handbook, a large and expensive reference book. The buyer paid only a nominal fee plus shipping and handling to get the handbook, and in exchange was enrolled in the club with a commitment to buy a few additional books. The publisher felt the handbook was such an attractive incentive that they featured it on the outer envelope of the promotion with this teaser: “Why are we giving away this 50th Anniversary Edition of Perry’s Handbook practically for free?” An advertisement for an application development tool used by programmers used the headline: “Develop applications up to 6X faster — guaranteed or your money back.” Putting the guarantee in the headline helps address skepticism for a big promise right up front. Not necessarily writing the copy … but agonizing over what has been written. As a copywriter, I do this all the time. I fret to an insane degree over every sentence, reading the copy over and over again, questioning whether the wording could be stronger. Many marketers do the same thing. They mark change after change on a nearly finished promotion, worrying about whether the copy says exactly the right thing, in exactly the right way. The irony, of course, is that in most situations, all this suffering is for naught. I don’t mean to say that copy is unimportant. But most of the time, the changes we make — punctuation, grammar, spelling, and minor word choice (e.g., whether to use “the” or “a”) — are so insignificant, it wouldn’t make one iota of difference in response whether we went with “version A” or “version B.” That said, I do think you should put in the time to carefully fine-tune your promotion … but only a small fraction of it. Specifically, here are the three “hot spots” in your promotion where what you say — and how you say it — really, really matters: The first critical portion of the copy is determined by its position in the promotion. The most important copy in a #10 direct-mail package is the outer envelope teaser — and the headline and lead of the sales letter. In a magalog, it’s the front cover … the inside front cover … the headline and lead … and the back cover. On a landing page, it’s the banner, headline, salutation, and lead. In an e-mail, it’s the subject line and the first paragraph. These sections are worth agonizing over, because different wording can result in dramatic increases or decreases in your response rates. Given the importance of the headline, should it focus on the offer instead of the product or the prospect? But that means the best-performing team in professional baseball still lost four out of every 10 games it played. And remember: That was the best record in baseball at the time. What’s ironic is that businesspeople who accept this statistical fact about baseball without a second thought … absolutely go bonkers when even one of their marketing programs fails. Experienced direct marketers know — and expect — that a percentage of their test campaigns will under-perform the control or even lose money. They accept this fact without despair, because they know that if one test mailing in every two … or every three … or even every five is a winner — they can make a lot of money. Inexperienced direct marketers don’t get this, however. As a result, countless small businesses test direct-marketing offers only once every few years, making it difficult if not impossible to identify the winning offer — the one offer that can multiply their sales two, three, even fivefold or more. If they don’t hit a home run the first time at bat, they loudly proclaim that “direct marketing doesn’t work” … and abandon it wholesale. If you’re a business owner or marketing professional, is there a better way to get direct marketing to work for you? Yes. Simply do more testing — of offers, reply elements, copy, prices — than you do right now. Let’s say you are planning to mail 5,000 postcards to drive people to a Web page. You just can’t decide which of two headlines you like — “Tastes Great” vs. “Less Filling.” If you subjectively pick just one, your risk of selecting the wrong sales appeal — and, therefore, having your postcard mailing bomb — is 50 percent. A much better approach is to split the postcard mailing into two batches, half with the headline “Tastes Great” and the other half with “Less Filling.” _________________________ “Don’t let personal preferences get in the way. Especially on the Web, testing variations — of headlines, copy, graphics, formats, and offers — is relatively quick, easy, and inexpensive. I am amazed at how many marketers, large and small, online and offline, invest significant sums in developing products — and then promote each product with just a single promotion … with no testing of any kind. If you are doing this, you are essentially hoping you’ll get a hit with only once chance at bat. In baseball, a .250 hitter who gets only one at-bat has a one in four chance of getting on base. In reality, for product launches, the success rate is often as low as 10 percent — which means that a single promotion has only a one in 10 chance of making money. That makes the odds of winning with a one-shot promotion 10 to one against you. _________________________ “Advertising arguments should only be settled by testing, not arguments around a conference table.” — Claude Hopkins _________________________ By testing different copy, offers, designs, and formats, you can significantly tip those odds in your favor. Giving your marketing multiple chances to score a winner is clearly the way to go. Copywriter Peter Betuel advises marketers: Don’t let personal preferences get in the way. What’s important is not what you think, like, believe, or prefer … it’s what your prospects think, like, believe, and prefer. No one can predict which offer will work best, and the least effective way to make marketing decisions is through subjective judgment. But as a direct marketer, you don’t have to rely on subjective judgment. You can put almost any proposition — e.g., offer “A” vs. offer “B,” or long copy vs. short copy — to a direct test with a statistically valid A/B split. For instance, a company that rented automobiles by the week tested two offers. Offer “A” was a free upgrade to a larger size model. Offer “B” was a rental discount given in exchange for purchasing multiple weeks of rentals in advance. (Customers would get a book of tickets they could redeem at the car counter.) To almost everyone’s surprise, offer “B” outperformed offer “A” significantly, generating nearly a tenfold increase in revenues. As advertising legend Claude Hopkins once said: “Advertising arguments should only be settled by testing, not arguments around a conference table.” And that includes the answer to the question: Which offer is best? In Conclusion … The way an offer is worded and presented is tremendously important. The right offer can boost response rates by 10 to 900 percent. The more you stress your offer in your promotional copy, the more leads and orders you will generate. Testing different prices and terms can yield big improvements in sales, and the results are often surprising. For example, the lower price is frequently not the winner of the test. The easiest way to increase response rates is to offer a premium — a free gift with order or inquiry. Free information — e.g., a free special report, CD, or video — can work extremely well as a premium. Guarantees should be at least 60 and preferably 90 days, and they should be unconditional. (Return the product and you get your money back.) Create a sense of urgency by giving the prospect a deadline or other incentive to respond to your offer now instead of later. Design your offer so all the risk is on the seller’s shoulders, not the buyer’s. Make buying entirely risk-free. You can never predict which offer will get the best response. Only by doing a series of A/B split tests will you find the winning offer for your product or service.
